name: Ajayi Collins Enesi
missingPieces: D1 omits unsalted MD5 hashing (A02/CWE-916) and the cookie missing Secure/SameSite finding (A05/CWE-614); open redirect appears only in D3. The actual safe decoy (HS256 hash_equals constant-time branch / b64url helpers) is never identified. D2 has no naira impact figure and skips the stored-XSS and open-redirect hops; SQLi CVSS uses A:H instead of A:N. D4 cites NDPA but with no section number (s.40 72h notify, s.41 data-subject notice).
feedback: D1: You catalogued seven of the ten findings with quoted artefact lines and mostly correct classes, which is solid evidence discipline. SQL injection (A03/CWE-89 at login.php ln62-67), the hardcoded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 (CWE-798), missing exp claims (CWE-613), XXE (CWE-611 with the file:///etc/passwd entity), path traversal (CWE-22 at the 02:24:02 capture) and the stored XSS beacon to 185.220.101.9 are all well evidenced. You missed unsalted MD5 as its own finding (A02/CWE-916 at ~ln66), the cookie missing Secure/SameSite (A05/CWE-614 at ~ln86), and you only put open redirect in D3. The decoy section is where you lost the most: the genuinely safe construct in this pack is the HS256 verify branch that uses hash_equals(), which is constant-time and sound, plus the b64url encode helpers. You instead nominated alg:none as the trap and then argued it is a real bug, which is correct about alg:none but means you never identified or disproved the actual decoy, so that six-point row scored zero. To be clear you did not fabricate anything, you just analysed the wrong construct. D2: The chain is in roughly the right shape (SQLi to JWT forgery to XXE/file read to the 312-row export) with verbatim PoCs for each hop you kept, but you dropped the stored-XSS (02:18:47) and open-redirect (02:21:13) hops and did not reconcile every step to its capture timestamp in order. Your SQLi vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H scores A:H, but an auth bypass does not hit availability, so it should be A:N for about 9.1. Your chain vector with S:C at 10.0 was the right instinct because the forged super_admin token reaches the shared /api/v1/internal service. The biggest D2 gap is impact: you stated 312 customers but gave no naira, and the key wanted you to reason from balances up to ~950k NGN summing to tens of millions, stating assumptions rather than declining to quantify. D3: The exec summary is clear and jargon-free and the threat model is genuine, and your two detection stopgaps name exact fields (username POST body, Authorization header / legacy_admin_jwt cookie, alg==none) with false-positive rates. Your remediation order is risk-and-initial-access led rather than strictly by CVSS, which is acceptable, though a true effort-first ordering would have promoted the low-effort XXE disable above the medium-effort SQLi and JWT rebuilds. The decoy statement in D3 is wrong: you named the open redirect as the disproved decoy, but open redirect is a real finding (#9, A01/CWE-601) and the actual decoy is the safe hash_equals branch, so that row scored zero. D4: Strong work here. You answered all four prompts in your own voice, cited ISC2 Canons 1, 2 and 3 load-bearing, and anchored to the confirmed customer-data exposure. The one miss is that you referenced the NDPA without a section number, so cite NDPA 2023 s.40 (notify NDPC within 72 hours) and s.41 (notify the 312 data subjects on high risk) to make it load-bearing. I looked for a way to round you into the 70s and the evidence did not support it: the missing MD5 and cookie findings, the unidentified decoy in both D1 and D3, and the absent naira impact each cost real points rather than being borderline judgment calls. The single most important fix is to learn the decoy: prove the hash_equals constant-time branch safe at the mechanism level instead of flagging a real bug as the trap, and never mislabel a real finding like open redirect as the decoy.
